title: Article 370: Dr. Ambedkar's Principled Stand on Constitutional Reciprocity
summary: In widely recounted accounts originating from contemporary memoirs, Dr. Ambedkar is reported to have expressed strong principled reservations regarding asymmetric constitutional provisions for Jammu & Kashmir, arguing that union rights require reciprocal citizenship obligations.
full_text:
During the drafting of India's Constitution in late 1949, intense discussions unfolded regarding the constitutional relationship between the Indian Union and the princely state of Jammu & Kashmir.

According to historical recollections recorded in contemporary memoirs by observer Balraj Madhok, Kashmiri leader Sheikh Abdullah met with Law Minister Dr. B. R. Ambedkar to discuss special autonomous provisions for the state.

As related in those accounts, Ambedkar expressed severe constitutional reservations upon reviewing the proposed terms:

"Examine what is being proposed:
You expect the Indian Union to defend your borders with its armed forces;
You expect national resources to build highways and support public infrastructure;
Yet you propose that the Indian Parliament shall have limited jurisdiction, and that citizens from other parts of the Union shall not enjoy equal reciprocal rights.
A durable constitutional relationship must be founded upon mutual equality and shared responsibilities."

Whether through this reported meeting or broader cabinet deliberations, it is historically established that Dr. Ambedkar declined to take legislative charge of drafting the special article.

Prime Minister Jawaharlal Nehru consequently entrusted the responsibility of piloting Article 370 (introduced in the Constituent Assembly as Article 306A) to Minister without Portfolio N. Gopalaswami Ayyangar, who steered it through the assembly on October 17, 1949.

Ambedkar's stance reflected his lifelong legal philosophy: that true constitutional democracy thrives on equal citizenship, reciprocal rights, and uniform fundamental guarantees for every citizen.
moral: Constitutional covenants must balance rights with responsibilities; asymmetric privileges undermine national solidarity.

authenticity_note: This dialogue originates from the memoirs of contemporary political observer Balraj Madhok. While it is historically verified that N. Gopalaswami Ayyangar—and not Law Minister Ambedkar—steered Article 370 (initially Article 306A) through the Constituent Assembly, this specific private exchange does not appear in official Constituent Assembly Debates and is regarded by historians as an attributed memoir account rather than an official verbatim transcript.
